title: Emergent edgecase LLM API battlemap
content:
Context:
This is a compact, tactical battlemap focused on non-obvious objection vectors and edge-case traps that field teams run into when positioning Redwood vs general LLM API providers. Meant for AEs, SEs, and product-aligned SDR/CS reps. Not a polished slide — working notes and scripts.

High-level thesis:
- Customers care loudly about access to capabilities, but actually choose based on predictable economics, fallback behavior, and operational simplicity when things go wrong.
- Our sweet spot: teams that need production predictability (latency SLOs, rollout safety, private deployments) and don’t want to build heavy ops around models.

Target personas & signals to listen for:
- Platform/Infra leads: mention of "SLA", "VPC", "private endpoints", "KMS", or rooftop concerns about data egress.
- Product/Feature managers: emphasis on iteration speed, API ergonomics, and deterministic output quality.
- ML Engineers/SREs: bringing up batching/kv-cache, perf regressions after quantization, and tail latency.
- Finance/Procurement: unit economics, reserved capacity, predictable line items.

Core messaging pillars (short pull-quotes):
- "Predictable inference economics: configurable batching + KV caching to control spend without guessing."
- "Unified runtime from hosted to on-prem — same API, fewer surprises during migration."
- "Production-grade fallbacks and rollout policies — keep apps online when a model or region hiccups."

Feature comparison talking points (ripped into quick bullets so reps can riff):
- Latency predictability: many LLM APIs optimize for avg latency. We prioritize percentile SLAs (configurable) + local KV caching to cut tails. Lead with behavior not raw mean numbers.
- Billing transparency: some vendors hide committed vs burst rates; emphasize our clear reserved vs metered model and examples (how reserved capacity smooths billing).
- Rollouts & rollbacks: rivals often lack first-class canary/A-B for model variants. Explain Redwood's canary step-down and automatic fallback to compatible variants.
- Private deployments: not all providers offer a private control plane + on-prem option with KMS integration. Call out compliance/regulators as win conditions.
- Observability: token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route tracing hooks — tie to debugging slowness and tail-cost surprises.
- Cost controls: intelligent batching / quantization recommendations — present as config knobs rather than black-box tuning.

Edge-case traps and scripts (how reps should handle specific tricky objections):
1) "Your latency numbers are cherry-picked — give me p99 for 4k contexts."
   - Reply: "Totally fair. We publish percentile profiles and sample traces. In our experience p99 is sensitive to sequence-length distribution and batching settings; let’s run a short eval with your traffic profile and show p50/p95/p99 under two config sets (low-latency vs batch-optimized)."
   - Demo ask: bring a 30-minute sandbox with a recorded request distribution.

2) "We can do this ourselves on cloud GPUs cheaper than your API."
   - Reply: "Self-hosting reduces per-token list price but increases ops tax: rollout safety, metric-driven regressions, kernel tuning, and 24/7 incident ops. We break down total cost of ownership across three axes: infra, engineering time, and risk (downtime/regression impact)."
   - Objection-close: offer a 6-week proof-of-value with a scripted failover scenario and measured ops time saved.

3) "We need an air-gapped solution — can you guarantee no outbound telemetry?"
   - Reply: "Yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed control planes and optional air-gapped installs. If it’s a hard requirement, we can walk through our checklist and red-team the telemetry surfaces in a pre-sales security review."

4) "Your quantized models sound risky for quality-sensitive features."
   - Reply: "We recommend model-specific quantization profiles and automated evals on your prompt corpus. We’ll show delta reports and rollback triggers if quality dips beyond a threshold — not a swap-and-forget approach."

Technical rebuttals / SE-ready notes (for deep dives):
- Batching: explain continuous batching vs synchronous single-request pipelines. Share how keeping small-time windows + sequence-length histograms reduces cold-start penalty.
- KV cache: highlight prefix-KV caching for chat — show a micro-example where repeated context reduces token generation by X% for a sample session (use customer data in sandbox).
- Kernel selection: point to runtime heuristics that pick quantization-friendly kernels and how that retains performance across hardware generations.
- Fallback routing: show sequence diagram of request -> primary rack -> fallback to variant with compatibility shim and how stateful sessions are preserved.

Demo & playbook checklist (10-minute quick demo flow):
- 0:00–1:00: One-sentence problem statement + customer signals.
- 1:00–3:00: Show Console: route-level latency & cost breakdown, a recent regression alert tied to a prompt set.
- 3:00–6:00: Live generate: same prompt against two model variants with quantization on/off; show p95 traces.
- 6:00–8:00: Open the rollout UI and simulate a canary failover to fallback model; show latency and success metrics after failover.
- 8:00–10:00: Ask for next step: data share for a short eval or a technical workshop.

Proof points & positioning data (phrased as claims you can stand behind):
- Use internal evals/benchmarks for examples rather than absolute claims: "In our internal evaluation on customer-like chat traffic, switching from default batching to workload-aware batching reduced token spend by ~22% while holding p95 latency within 15%."
- Call out partner references: "Customer X (SaaS) used dedicated capacity to guarantee 99% of in-office transactions under their 200ms latency target during business hours."

Collateral to carry into deals (ask marketing to prioritize):
- Short 1-pager: "Why reserved capacity saves dev time" (customer story + cost math).
- Play-by-play demo script (condensed for SDRs).
- Technical note: "How Redwood does canary rollouts for LLMs" (sequence diagrams + rollback triggers).

Escalation triggers (when to pull in product-eng/research):
- Customer has unusual token shapes (e.g., very long-context convo + high concurrency).
- Needs a model we don’t support yet — ask product for compatibility plan within 72 hours.
- Asks for formal SOC2/PenTest artifacts beyond current pack — escalate to security/compliance.

Competitive signals (listen for these in discovery):
- If they mention another vendor’s "free tier throughput" + "no-hosting cost", they likely focus on unit price over ops risk.
- If they name an incumbent that sells both infra and model hosting, prepare differentiation on portability and unified API.

Open questions (for product and exec briefing):
- Do we have a short checklist/one-pager for legal on data residency for Private installs?
- Can we publish a short "how we measure latency p95/p99" doc for sales to reference?

Next steps for this doc (quick TODOs):
- SEs: convert technical rebuttals into 2–3 snippet scripts for playbook. (Owner: Ravi)
- Marketing: produce the 1-pager and demo-script. (Owner: Marta)
- Prod: confirm support SLA language for rollbacks and private installs; add to knowledge base. (Owner: Evan)

Notes to self:
- Keep this file lightweight — rotate quarterly with new win stories.
- Avoid publishing raw latency numbers in public collateral; use ranges and customer examples with permission.

End of notes.
